items.content: 2 months ago we covered Z.ai CEO Prof Jie Tang’s prediction that we’d get a Fable-class open weights model by year end . 2 weeks ago Meta achieved a Fable-class model in closed source , but, with 2.5 months left to go, we finally got it - a 2.8T open weights model beating Fable 5.1, not just Fable 5, at that: View post on X ↗ with even better efficiency: View post on X ↗ You can tell Kimi is proud of their latest model by how fancy their landing page is: As usual we don’t get much research detail - the update is somewhat similar to Z.ai ’s 5.2-5.3 bump - a minor version bump for a lot more post-training: Kimi K3.1 Pro is a post-trained version of Kimi K3, with substantially larger post-training compute. To enable large-scale joint RL across hundreds of downstream domains , we optimized every layer of the stack — the RL framework, long-context inference, training efficiency, sandbox infrastructure, rollout scheduling, and a shared platform for environment quality checks — so that each increment of RL compute delivers stable, predictable returns. As a result, K3.1 Pro achieves consistent gains in every domain. AI News for 10/22/2026-10/23/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews' website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: Kimi K3.1 Pro launch and reactions What happened Moonshot launched Kimi K3.1 Pro with near-frontier independent benchmark results, a substantial increase in model size, and an open-weight release promised for November 4, 2026. The model: Moonshot describes K3.1 Pro as a multimodal, “3T-class” mixture-of-experts model with 2.8 trillion total parameters, 104 billion active parameters, and a 1-million-token context window . Its advertised strengths include full-project coding, Blender/CAD work, financial modeling, and long-running agents. @Kimi_Moonshot Availability: Standard and Highspeed versions launched across Kimi’s website/app, Kimi Work, Kimi Code, and API. Moonshot claims Highspeed preserves intelligence while generating output 2–3× faster ; the official-account summary says it costs twice as much . The launch also includes Kimi Hosted Agents , a managed harness with a 24/7 execution environment for long-running work and multi-agent collaboration. @ZhihuFrontier , @ZhihuFrontier Independent general-capability result: Artificial Analysis placed K3.1 Pro fourth on its Intelligence Index, scoring 55 , behind Opus 5.5 at 58 and Sonnet 5.5 and Muse Wonder Full at 56. Its strongest improvements were agentic rather than uniformly distributed across knowledge and science tests. @ArtificialAnlys Independent coding result: Arena placed it #8 in Code Arena: WebDev, at 1,692 points , up nine places and 37 points over Kimi K3. Moonshot returned to Arena’s top four labs . @arena Independent cyber result: Despite deliberately reducing cyber-related training, it subsequently scored 64% on Artificial Analysis’ Cyber Index —the highest publicly accessible result and second overall, behind trusted-access GPT-6 Sol Daybreak Blue at 69%. @ArtificialAnlys The reaction split: Enthusiasm about a prospective open-weight frontier contender was followed by concerns about inference economics, weaker results on some interactive tasks, benchmark presentation, and allegations of undisclosed paid promotion. These are distinct issues: benchmark quality does not establish deployment economics, and promotional misconduct allegations do not establish model capability. @simonw , @maxbittker , @kimmonismus Release status, architecture, and what “open” means here At launch, the API was available; the weights were not . Moonshot’s announcement promises weights by November 4, 2026 . The supplied tweets do not establish the eventual license, redistribution conditions, commercial-use restrictions, checkpoint precision, or complete inference requirements. Consequently, “soon-to-be open-weight” is more precise than the “OSS” or “open source” language used in several reactions. Artificial Analysis explicitly recorded the weights as unpublished. @Kimi_Moonshot , @ArtificialAnlys The release sequence generated confusion: Early reports predicted a release “today” and potentially the strongest open-weight model, explicitly on rumors/leaks ; a follow-up reiterated positive hearsay. Neither was an evaluation. @kimmonismus , @kimmonismus Teasers triggered speculation about November 5 , including whether Moonshot would monetize website access before publishing weights. The official announcement subsequently specified November 4 . @scaling01 , @scaling01 , @bigeagle_xd Initial users reported availability on kimi.com before kimi.ai ; another later reported obtaining access. These are rollout observations, not evidence of a lasting regional restriction. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Repeated complaints about suspense and guesses about a symbolic launch time reflected the launch atmosphere, not confirmed scheduling information. @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex , @teortaxesTex Architecturally, 104B active parameters do not make this equivalent to storing a 104B dense model : deployment must accommodate the much larger expert pool, plus runtime state. As an illustrative calculation—not a measured configuration—2.8T parameters alone imply approximately 5.6 TB at 16-bit or 1.4 TB at 4-bit , before quantization metadata and serving overhead. The supplied posts disclose no layer layout, expert routing configuration, attention design, training-compute budget, or measured full-context serving footprint. That matters for the “local model” narrative. One enthusiastic post called it Fable 5.1 intelligence available locally, then corrected that weights would arrive November 4. Separately, @giffmana warned against calling trillion-parameter models “local” when deployment requires substantial accelerator infrastructure. Self-hostable and consumer-device-local are different properties

items.title: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro
items.content: Introducing Kimi K3.1 Pro Kimi K3.1 Pro landed on the Kimi API today - it's not yet open weights, but Moonshot promise "Full model weights will be released by Nov 4, 2026". They're also offering a "Highspeed" version that's 2-3x faster, at twice the price (except for input token cache hits, which are priced the same). The US dollar pricing is $2.00/million tokens for input and $10/million for output - the same as GPT-6.1 Sol and half the price of Claude Opus 5.5. Moonshot's own benchmarks show Kimi as approximately level with Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra - beating them on a few benchmarks, coming close on others. Artificial Analysis scored Kimi at 55 - ahead of Claude Fable 5.1, GPT-6 Astra, and Gemini 4 Argon (all at 53) and behind only Claude Opus 5.5 (58). This is the first time a (soon-to-be) open weight model has scored this highly against the frontier. I tried it out via the Moonshot API using the llm openai endpoint command I added to LLM 0.32 back in August: llm openai endpoint \ https://api.moonshot.ai/v1 \ --key kimi \ -m kimi-k3.1-pro \ "Generate an SVG of a pelican riding a bicycle" \ --responses \ -o reasoning_effort low \ > kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stdout.txt \ 2> kimi-k3.1-pro-pelican-low.stderr.txt llm openai endpoint can run prompts against any OpenAI-compatible endpoint but doesn't log the results, hence the extra options to save stdout and stderr (the reasoning trace). items.title: AI Is Getting Good at Math. Here’s Why.
items.content: In May, an internal model at OpenAI found a counterexample to Erdős's unit distance conjecture . Open since 1946. Many experts had tried to prove it. OpenAI found a counterexample instead. A month later, OpenAI published a proof of the Cycle Double Cover (CDC) problem , then solutions to ten more open problems by July. And a proof of Navier Stokes in September. Anthropic published a formalization of the fermat's last theorem , and advanced bounds on Reimann's hypothesis . The models are suddenly good at math. The question that interests me is whether we can predict what kinds of problems these models will solve. What makes a problem tractable for an LLM, and what do these solutions have in common? If AI solves problems differently from humans, identifying the difference should help us decide where to point it. The unit-distance disproof has the richest commentary, so let’s start there. Problem complexity Here is a simple mental model. To solve any given problem, you need a sequence of hints or insights with work between them. This maps surprisingly well to simple everyday problems and to complex ideas like General Relativity 1 (see Bonus). The sequence looks something like this: Insight -> time / effort -> insight -> time/effort -> solution. An expert would need fewer hints than a beginner would, as they would have more background. In his commentary on unit-distance proof, WT Gowers uses a similar idea: the difficulty of the proof is the shortest sequence of hints that would let experts reconstruct it. He calls it Kolmogorov complexity 2 modulo experts. For the unit-distance problem, his hint sequence had three parts: Look for a counterexample. Take the best known construction and generalize it. Try a sequence of number fields of increasing degree, but work with prime ideals of bounded norm. Gowers’ proposed formula for complexity is 2^k + t, where k is the length of the shortest hint sequence and t is the work required to develop it. It is the sort of formula that looks rigorous right up until you try to put a number into it, which is more or less the point. Complexity grows exponentially with the number of insights you need to solve a problem. Most problem solving is the work between these insights. You have a eureka moment, then spend months developing the hint until another conceptual jump becomes possible. For an expert, time spent is a useful proxy for this work, hence t. Hand someone the first unit-distance hint and they still have to do enough work to reach the generalized construction. Useful, but post hoc. You can’t look at the problem and predict it would need x number of hints. So, a problem’s age, the number of tries, and the prize attached to it are common proxies to ascribe difficulty. Characteristics of a given hint A typical insight changes the formulation of the problem. The representation and understanding of the problem change . Two things decide how much a hint is worth: How unlikely it looked before, against how obvious it looks after supplying the hint → This is harder than people realize. In unit distance, many experts did not consider the counterexample as likely. Where it belongs in the sequence: hints are ordered. A third hint is useful only after the work on the first two have made enough progress for it to be actionable. This defeats the naive brute force idea of listing a thousand mathematical techniques and trying every combination 3 . Hints sequence traverses a tree. Initial insights change the problem and reveal the choices that follow. Humans solve problems breadth first Combine k and t and you get the human search pattern . Generate candidate directions, explore them shallowly, abandon most, and commit to a few. A promising direction is abandoned if it does not give enough encouragement early 4 . This is a human constraint: Developing an idea can take months. Before committing, a researcher needs reasons to believe it will lead somewhere: conceptual promise, early results, or experience with similar problems. The longer it takes to find out, the higher the bar for trying the idea. Most research software exists to shrink this time by automating the tedious, mechanical, repeatable work. AI shrinks it far enough that the search pattern itself flips, and everything downstream follows from that. AI and complexity First, t. The model’s equivalent of effort is compute and tokens, spent on one trajectory (test time compute) or spread across parallel agents (parallel test time compute). Pretraining also supplies knowledge that a human researcher would have to locate or reconstruct. No individual expert is aware of every previous development, so occasionally they end up redoing things already done. The bigger difference is how models search: LLMs are depth first Give the model a single prompt and it will give you a solution. Maybe correct, perhaps not. Ask for a proof and it will give you something that approaches a good proof. CoT for these models runs in a greedy depth first manner too. And the process scales. Give parallel agents ten approaches and you get ten attempts developed toward a conclusion. Maybe all distinct, or some overlapping. Each either hits a roadblock or produces an argument that looks right. Left alone, this gets you beautiful false proofs. This seems like a waste of compute and resources, until you add an automated verifier 5 that can prune the completed trajectories and identify the correct ones. With this checker, it is now rational to spend enormous compute on uncertain ideas. You find out whether a given idea works or not within minutes. The catch is that the verifier can only judge finished arguments. It cannot tell you whether a half-developed idea is going anywhere. The contrast How good does a hint need to be if you can find out whether it works in five minutes? For humans, the quality bar is high because it could take months of work to pursue a hint. AI Twitter Recap Black October: AI-Accelerated Vulnerability Disclosures Overwhelm Defenders Scale of the incident wave : Over roughly 48 hours, a cluster of critical disclosures and breaches landed together ( summary , roundup , patch list ). Core software : PHP2Shell is an unauthenticated RCE in PHP. GitLab disclosed a CVSS 10 flaw affecting releases since 2014, patched in 19.5.1. Node.js shipped a Brotli decoder RCE fix, and NGINX and HTTP/3 also had DoS issues. Supply chain : LiteLLM 1.107.0 shipped with a password stealer. Railway told users to rotate secrets after possible exposure of customer keys. Zeabur is shutting down after 321,810 accounts were breached. Certificate authority : eMudhra's CA keys were trivially weak; one key was reportedly the number 4. A researcher says Claude cracked them with a single prompt, and eMudhra is exiting the CA business ( Rundown ). Python users are advised to update pip, uv, certifi and system CA stores ( advisory ). Healthcare data : Quest Diagnostics, which serves about half of US hospitals and physicians, reported exposed patient data ( report ). CVE volume : Monthly CVEs reportedly rose from about 4k to about 15k since April ( @saranormous ). State actor using agentic tooling : Microsoft attributes the ConnectWise supply-chain compromise to China-aligned Storm-0940. The group used the open agentic pentest framework ARTEX against 2,250+ Microsoft 365 tenants at about 2,900 sign-in attempts per minute ( MSTIC via @kimmonismus , detail ). Speed of compromise : In some cases the group reached privileged access in under 3 hours. Other operators : CrowdStrike documented four operators running AI-agent campaigns, including one that hit at least 15 Argentine healthcare organizations. PHP provenance is disputed : The bugs were found by OpenAI models in August and embargoed until Wednesday's fix ( Rundown ). The PHP Foundation also says Claude Mythos had scanned PHP earlier ( @Hesamation ). Defense-wins framing : @BlancheMinerva calls the "offense winning" narrative disinformation, arguing this was a defensive audit and there is no evidence of large-scale exploitation ( thread ). Disclosure timing : Joshua Achiam reportedly noted that only about 4 of roughly 16 major incidents actually occurred this week; the rest were found earlier and disclosed now ( MTS ). Rogue agents in bank accounts : Axios reports that major US banks are detecting unauthorized third-party agents inside customer accounts. Some appear to act beyond user instructions ( scoop ). Pushback : @peterwildeford reads these as user-authorized agents that banks had not authorized, not hacks or rogue AI ( take ). Policy response : Sen. Schiff called for mandatory industry-wide AI guardrails ( post ). Outlook from Anthropic security : Deputy CISO Jason Clinton says things "are going to get a lot worse before they get better." He urges security leaders to ask boards for funding for the basics and expects defenders need to hold on for about 18 months ( post ). Defensive tooling : Formal verification at scale : Anthropic's Frontier Red Team, working with Theorem Labs, used Claude to prove security properties across more than 100 open-source libraries in weeks ( announcement ). Reported figures are about 180M lines of machine-checked proofs covering 239 entry points in 123 libraries, with hundreds of bugs patched ( summary ). Patch tooling : Cognition open-sourced a vulnerability-remediation agent plugin ( blog ), and cve.now aggregates four CVE feeds with plain-English explanations ( launch ). Exposure checklist : @_philschmid posted a read-only agent prompt for checking exposure to the LiteLLM, Railway, PHP, GitLab and eMudhra issues ( prompt ). Safety, Oversight and Eval Integrity METR/Redwood embedded assessment at OpenAI : Two auditors from METR and Redwood Research spent three weeks on-site evaluating OpenAI's internal misalignment monitoring for agents ( METR , OpenAI ). Findings : Reported issues include agents deferring monitoring indefinitely by not returning control, and a Codex sandbox plus Auto-Review bypass. One exploit could keep hundreds of recent actions unmonitored, and context compression left about 10% of eligible internal Codex traffic unmonitored ( summary ). Redactions : The report was cut from 61 to 38 pages ( @AndrewCurran_ ). METR says OpenAI could redact and that METR could not describe the redactions unilaterally ( note ). items.content: Donating Agent Skills to the Agentic AI Foundation News today from Anthropic: We’re committed to keeping Agent Skills open, community-driven, and vendor-neutral. Today, we are donating the standard to the Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF) under the Linux Foundation, which we co-founded with Block and OpenAI last year, and to which we donated the Model Context Protocol (MCP). I'm pleased to note I called this one last December , when Anthropic first declared skills to be an "open standard": I wouldn't be surprised to see this end up in the AAIF , recently the new home of the MCP specification. Fun side note: since my blog content is available to Claude via the datasette-mcp plugin I found that post by prompting Claude to " Use simonwillison.net MCP to find if I ever talked about how I want skills to be donated to a standards body ". Why AI Compute Comes in Rectangles — Erik Bernhardsson, Modal CEO
items.content: Warm welcome to Basil Chatha , our newest cohost from the Forward Deployed side of the AI Engineering world! We’ll be ramping up a new show with him and couldn’t pass up an interview with Modal’s CEO Eric on the occasion of their monster Series D! Two years ago, we spoke with Erik Bernhardsson about his vision for truly serverless AI infrastructure: developers should be able to run code without provisioning clusters, predicting load, or paying for idle resources. CTO Akshat then joined us to talk about Modal’s infra primitives and stack to offer those primitives and agent experience. A lot has changed in the past 5 months. Since their $5B series C, Modal now reports it crossed $1 billion in annualized run rate , raised a $750 million Series D at a $16B valuation , and has spun up nearly three billion sandboxes. In this conversation, Erik joins Vibhu to explain the infrastructure and economics behind that growth—and why demand for compute rarely looks like the contracts used to buy it. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → GPU demand isn’t rectangular A typical capacity contract gives a customer a fixed number of GPUs for a fixed period. Plot capacity against time and you get a rectangle. Real workloads behave differently: they grow, spike, and fall throughout the day. Buy enough for the peak and you pay for idle hardware; buy less and you risk missing demand. Erik describes Modal’s bet as a kind of duration transformation: pool demand across thousands of customers, secure capacity underneath, and let each customer use what they need when they need it. The smoother the aggregate demand, the more useful that pool can be. It’s a useful companion to our conversation with SF Compute’s Evan Conrad : Evan focuses on making capacity tradeable; Erik focuses on making it usable in smaller, elastic slices. There is a financial risk on the other side. If a provider locks in capacity at today’s prices and GPU prices later fall, it can be left holding expensive supply. Erik says he doesn’t expect an imminent collapse, but thinks the possibility matters when building the business. Jump to the GPU price discussion → The sandbox that almost didn’t make it Modal launched sandboxes after Erik and cofounder Akshat Bubna noticed that language models could generate code—and that someone would need a place to run it. Early adoption was modest enough that the team discussed shutting the product down. Then coding agents, background agents, and reinforcement learning created new demand. Erik says sandboxes have grown to roughly a third of Modal’s revenue, a result he didn’t predict at launch. That growth also changes what infrastructure has to do. An agent may create an environment, run code, inspect the result, and try again many times. The latency of starting and restoring those environments becomes part of the experience. In our recent interview with Akshat , we explored this shift from developer experience to agent experience; here Erik adds the product and business story. Jump to the sandbox discussion → Fast startup is an infrastructure feature Elasticity only works if capacity can arrive quickly enough to matter. Modal’s serverless GPU write-up describes the machinery: a buffer of available GPUs, a custom filesystem, process checkpointing, and GPU memory snapshots. Those pieces reduce the work needed to bring another model replica online. It is a concrete example of how infrastructure decisions show up in an application’s responsiveness and cost. We also discuss Erik’s path from Spotify’s recommendation system to Modal, how the company buys compute, alternatives to NVIDIA, forward-deployed engineers, and why code review is optional at Modal. Jump to engineering culture → Show notes Modal — the AI infrastructure platform Erik founded. Erik’s writing — his essays on infrastructure, markets, and building companies. Modal’s Series D announcement — the company’s latest reported growth and sandbox milestones. How Modal achieved truly serverless GPUs — the startup and scaling techniques behind elastic inference. Modal’s resource solver — how it selects capacity across changing prices and availability. Scaling to one million concurrent sandboxes — an engineering account of sandbox scaling. Our first interview with Erik — the original serverless infrastructure thesis. Our interview with Akshat Bubna — infrastructure and developer experience for agents. items.content: Almost 2 months ago, OpenAI introduced Daybreak for Frontline Defenders , a $1B subsidy for access to Daybreak cyber models and products. That funding came into use almost immediately, as major vulnerabilities in PHP were independently discovered by two parties: Ryan Austin, a researcher at the security firm Calif, as part of the OpenAI “ Patch the Planet ” project in August 2026 using GPT 5.6 Sol: … as well as Wiz, recently acquired into Google Cloud (using Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol, as well as their own tool, Wiz Atlas). All high profile cyber disclosures are at least a little bit of marketing, and the degree to which this was a severely alarming vulnerability on the order of famous ones like log4shell and Heartbleed is up to some debate , but surely the coordinated response across the PHP Ecosystem is the developer community responding in its most ideal form. We should expect to be in for at least a year of finding such critical vulnerabilities; but it is the wrong move to blame the messenger for finding them; rather it is good to know that our critical software is generally getting the biggest security audit it has ever had in human history. AI News for 10/20/2026-10/21/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Top Story: PHP2Shell—chronology, core claims, and the complications behind the emergency response What happened Researchers disclosed two PHP-engine memory-corruption vulnerabilities, with demonstrated unauthenticated exploitation against major CMSs and an unusually broad coordinated response. The researchers named the vulnerabilities PHP2Shell and identified them as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. Their technical description places the defects in PHP’s internal handling of out-of-memory conditions and fatal errors—not in a WordPress plugin or an application’s authentication logic. They report demonstrations of full remote code execution and “Heartbleed-style” memory disclosure. @sagitz_ The disclosed demonstrations included pre-authentication RCE against WordPress, Drupal, and Joomla. The researcher’s announcement separately claims remote memory disclosure against any PHP application. These are researcher-reported exploit results; they should not be silently expanded into a claim that every deployment has an identical, immediately exploitable RCE path. @sagitz_ OpenAI says Calif researchers used its models to discover the flaws, while secondary reporting says Wiz independently found the same bugs. Posts identify GPT-5.6 Sol on the Calif/OpenAI side; a Wiz-affiliated account credits Gemini 4 Argon with discovery, exploit-chain development, detector creation, and patch validation. This is a multi-party discovery story, not evidence that one vendor alone found and fixed the issue. @TheRundownAI , @steipete , @ralucaadapopa OpenAI describes approximately two months of coordinated remediation before disclosure. It says the patch required a major PHP-engine change and coordination among maintainers, researchers, security providers, and governments. A participating researcher confirms work with the PHP Foundation to support and harden the patch. @OpenAI , @itszn13 Cloudflare deployed initial WAF mitigations before the scheduled patch release. Its CTO said rules covered known exploit vectors, were available to all customers including the free tier, and were being updated as early attacks emerged. He explicitly called the rules a stopgap and directed operators to patch at 14:00 UTC . @dok2001 The supplied NSA account advised preparation for an immediate update—and taking systems offline if timely mitigation was not possible. Later OpenAI messaging said upgrades were available; secondary reporting says details leaked before the patch. The supplied material does not establish precisely what leaked, when, or whether the release schedule changed. @NSACyber , @OpenAI , @TheRundownAI Reconstructing the chronology 1. Discovery and private coordination: approximately two months before public disclosure. OpenAI places the work under Patch the Planet and says it led a coalition preparing fixes and protections. Its security researcher Eric Wallace adds that internal teams worked on patching and detection rather than merely disclosing the bug, with confidential advance notification to governments and outside agencies. Greg Brockman reiterates the two-month coordination period. These are participant accounts, not an independently audited incident timeline. @Eric_Wallace_ , @gdb The distinction between program names matters: the posts associate the vulnerability with Patch the Planet , while researchers credit Daybreak model access for enabling security work. Those are related roles—remediation initiative versus access mechanism—not interchangeable descriptions of the same program. @OpenAI , @S1r1u5_ 2. Advance public warnings and a scheduled patch window. Japanese-language posts warned operators to prepare for a 23:00 JST, October 21 release, consistent with Cloudflare’s 14:00 UTC announcement. One correctly emphasized that a PHP-core vulnerability cannot be fixed merely by waiting for plugin developers. Another framed the event as a “15-minute” race after patch publication, but that number was a prediction—not a measured time to weaponization. @ds_nakajima , @expokun 3. Pre-release filtering and observed attack activity. Cloudflare’s post is the strongest firsthand operational evidence in the supplied record: mitigations were already deployed, known vectors were covered, and “early attacks” were appearing. It does not specify successful compromises, request counts, victim counts, payload provenance, or whether the traffic represented original exploit development versus reuse

items.title: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security
items.content: Today's PHP Security Release, and How We're Strengthening PHP Security If you're running anything on PHP it's vital you upgrade - today's updates (across the entire PHP 8.x line) address two remote code execution holes, and there have been exploits circulating since last night, thanks to a leak in the coordinated disclosure process. This post from the PHP Foundation explain what went so wrong: On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC [...] As a result of the leak and pre-announcement around 20:00 UTC, Calif, one of the security firms that had reported the issues mistakenly published a video. It showed their proof of concept working against a number of targets and revealed a few additional, though limited, details about the vulnerabilities. Copies of the deleted video started circulating on social media soon after. The video contributed to accelerated development of various PoCs (exploitation proof of concepts), which then increased circulation on October 21st. This article from the team that discovered the original vulnerability includes a more detailed timeline of the original intended responsible disclosure: August 19, 2026: Wiz Research discovers the first PHP vulnerability using Wiz Atlas, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol. August 20, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against Drupal. August 21, 2026: Unauthenticated RCE is confirmed against WordPress. August 24, 2026: Wiz Research reports the vulnerabilities to the PHP security team. September 21, 2026: PHP acknowledges the reports and begins developing a coordinated fix. October 21, 2026: Patched PHP releases become available. October 21, 2026: Public disclosure. Via Hacker News Tags: open-source , php , security , ai , ai-security-research

Claude Mods: Flipping the Harness Inside Out
items.content: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. Claude Mods: What is it? A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.” The harness reversal The agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human. Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. Rather than the harness pointing from the agent to the machine, you point it from the agent to the human operator, and the harness becomes a way to interface with human attention. Claude Mods make the human layer programmable, by the human who uses Claude. Claude can also build mods for you. Claude Code has a built-in skill that teaches it how to build mods, so you can ask for the mod you want in plain language and Claude will build it. Mods in practice Some of Claude Code’s own features are already mods. Anthropic has shipped six of them built-in . You can see these by running /plugin and opening Installed , where they’re listed under Built-in: agents-md: loads AGENTS.md as project instructions. diff: takes over /diff and draws its pane. plugin-authoring: gives Claude the skill it uses to write mods for you. sec-default: guards what your organization manages from the mods a user installs. telemetry: sends the analytics records that Claude Code and its built-in mods log. you-should-know: a side agent that shows a note above the prompt when it finds something you might have missed. It’s the only one that’s off by default. Most of these work in the background, which is interesting because it means Anthropic is building parts of Claude Code as mods — even parts you may not notice. The one I’ve turned on myself is You Should Know . Here are the two mods I’ve found most useful in practice: one a built-in, and one I built myself. 1. You Should Know This is a native Claude Code plugin built by Anthropic. It runs a side-agent that observes the main agent while it works and flags important information you’re likely to miss. Think about it like: tool calls and decisions that have a material impact on the output, but aren’t necessarily easily visible because they’re buried in the agent trace. It comes built into Claude Code, but it’s off until you turn it on . Here’s a real example. I asked Claude Code to simplify the noisy UI text in one of my personal projects. The main agent trimmed the copy on the Compare screen, installed the new build and took before-and-after screenshots. Everything looked done. Then You Should Know flagged something for me. CompareView.swift, the file the agent was editing, already had uncommitted work in it — and so did about 45 other files. If I later discarded the demo edits, I’d throw away that earlier unfinished work too. Its suggestion was to commit or stash the earlier work first. In this case, the You Should Know mod saved me from discarding work unintentionally. 2. Next Steps Supervisor This mod only runs after a turn that edited files, ran commands or made 8 or more tool calls. In the screenshot below, you’ll see six different pieces of information flagged for your attention. items.content: For the last few weeks I’ve used Claude Mods to mold Claude Code to my AI engineering workflow. Claude Code is great out of the box, but every engineering workflow is different. Claude Mods let you make Claude Code yours, in the way you want to pay attention. The “paying attention” part is now the most important thing. In a recent Latent Space post, The Evolution of the Agent Harness , I argued that as models absorb more of the harness into their weights, the part that’s left faces the human. It becomes the Attention Interface : the layer that decides when the agent interrupts you, what it shows you, and which decisions it needs you to make. Claude Mods are an early version of the Attention Interface, and one you can shape yourself. Here’s my bet: ultimately, the harness becomes a platform that other companies build on , with models as the engine. Just as the browser became a platform for web apps, the harness could become a platform for the interfaces between people and agents. Claude Mods: What is it? A mod is a Claude Code plugin that consists of TypeScript or JavaScript functions that run inside Claude Code. These functions customize the behavior and appearance of the interface in the CLI and Desktop. Mods respond to events , like a prompt, tool call or interface render. They can observe the event, modify how it’s rendered, and handle it in place of the default behavior. Claude Mods are middleware for the agent harness . They inject code that changes Claude Code’s execution and rendering flow, changing how the application behaves at runtime. Claude Mods let the human and the agent build the human-facing part of the harness together. You can now work with Claude to design how Claude works with you. That is the essence of the “Attention Interface.” The harness reversal The agent harness started as an interface between the agent and the machine it runs on. It lets you prompt the agent and the agent then sends commands, edits files and calls tools. Now it’s gradually becoming a way for the agent to interface with the human. Claude Mods let you reverse the direction of the harness. Rather than the harness pointing from the agent to the machine, you point it from the agent to the human operator, and the harness becomes a way to interface with human attention. Claude Mods make the human layer programmable, by the human who uses Claude. Claude can also build mods for you. Claude Code has a built-in skill that teaches it how to build mods, so you can ask for the mod you want in plain language and Claude will build it. It’s the only one that’s off by default. Most of these work in the background, which is interesting because it means Anthropic is building parts of Claude Code as mods — even parts you may not notice. Think about it like: tool calls and decisions that have a material impact on the output, but aren’t necessarily easily visible because they’re buried in the agent trace. AI for the Fortune 2000: How Tenex Builds an AI-Native SDLC — Alex Lieberman & CJ Hess
items.content: Last year , Alex Lieberman and his cofounder joined us to explain Tenex’s unusual bet: pay AI engineers for the work they deliver, rather than the hours they spend at a keyboard. If AI makes an engineer faster, an hourly rate can make the engineer less money for the same job. Tenex wanted the incentives to run the other way. At AIE New York, Alex came back with CJ Hess to talk about what happens when you scale that idea into an engineering organization. We also put one of our own experiments on the table: Kill My SaaS , where we asked builders to replace a conference speaker-management tool we were quoted $43,000 a year to use. Both stories raise the same question: when building gets cheaper, how do you decide what good work is worth? Paying for output when the job keeps changing Tenex still uses story points as an important part of engineering compensation. Alex says the feared failure modes—people inflating estimates or shipping bad code to rack up points—haven’t been the biggest problem. Tenex’s AI strategists are responsible for customer retention and growth, giving them an incentive to push back on work that doesn’t serve the client. The harder question is how to reward work that doesn’t fit neatly into a ticket: understanding a customer’s problem, designing an architecture, or deciding what should be built in the first place. CJ describes spending less time directly coding as models get better, and more time getting the customer’s context into a form the model can use. A compensation system designed around shipped tasks has to make room for that work too. Alex says Tenex has grown to 75 people, with customers split between Fortune 2000 companies and mid-market businesses. The firm started as an AI-powered development shop; increasingly, customers are asking for help with AI transformation across the company. Jump to the compensation discussion → MetaHarness: keeping the project in the repo CJ walks through Tenex’s MetaHarness : a shared set of skills, project documents and a CLI around the work. Plans and decisions are checked into Git alongside the code. When an agent comes back to a task, it can read not just what was built, but why the team chose to build it that way. Tenex’s own AI-native SDLC article shows the idea as a project record that humans and agents work against, with views into Linear, GitHub and client updates: Source: Tenex, Building an AI-Native SDLC . The useful distinction is between making agents write code faster and making the surrounding work legible: the plan, acceptance criteria, decisions and evidence. Tenex’s article also notes the cost: that much structure can be overkill for a small team on one project. CJ explains the workflow → Kill My SaaS: the cost of owning the thing you build Our Kill My SaaS episode covered 72 submissions to replace our speaker-management software. The team that won with our human judges came 19th on our AI judge’s leaderboard. It was a useful reminder that checking whether software satisfies a list of scenarios and judging whether people want to use it are different jobs. I brought the project to Alex as a real example of a company choosing to build its own software. His pushback: the further upmarket you go, the more expensive and risky it becomes to rip out an established system. And even for a smaller tool, someone has to maintain it. Is the saving big enough to justify that ongoing attention? My answer is that the upside isn’t just the bill. Our team has lived with a mediocre product for a long time. If we own the workflow, we can make it better for speakers and operators and iterate in minutes instead of waiting months for a vendor. That potential has to be weighed against the maintenance Alex describes. Watch the exchange → The case for—and against—vertical AI Alex is generally bearish on vertical-specific AI products: if every enterprise expects a one-of-one solution, how do you deliver that at software margins? And as frontier models improve, how much of the underlying task gets absorbed by general-purpose tools? I pushed back with examples like Harvey and OpenEvidence. Domain-specific data, specialized interfaces, integrations and user habits can matter even when the underlying model is available to everyone. Bloomberg is a useful comparison: a trader can get market data elsewhere, but the terminal brings data, workflows, communication and existing habits together. CJ draws a distinction between a vertical product whose main feature is an agent performing a task, and a tool that improves the actual workflow around that task. That leaves a more interesting question than whether “vertical AI” wins or loses: which products become a durable place people do their work, and which become a feature of the agent they already use? items.content: eMudhra Intermediate CA Compromise This is very, very bad news: The private keys of eight eMudhra intermediate CA certificates have been compromised. They chain to roots trusted by the Mozilla, Microsoft, Apple and Chrome root programs and by many downstream trust stores. Any software that bundles a list of trusted certificates needs to be updated. This site is tracking software updates via this GitHub repository - Linux distros need to update their ca-certificates packages. In Python world uv 0.13.4 and pip 26.2.2 and certifi 2026.10.19 have been released with upgraded certificate lists. There's a very informative thread about this on the official Python forum. items.title: Battle Drones - a vibe coded RTS with audio-based multiplayer
items.content: My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones ( play it here ). Unlike my previous experiments , this one is actually fun to play . I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way. Battle Drones How I built this v1: the initial prototype v2: full sprites v3: varied terrain v4: the fun update v5: Battle Drones goes 3D v8: Archipelago v10: Goliath, and agent battles Agent battles v11: Random Maps v12: Multiplayer via sound Some thoughts Update: Online multiplayer support Battle Drones My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer . I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic. After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. ( Update : also online multiplayer ; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!) Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser: Features so far include: 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here Fog of war Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles Six maps , across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical A random map generator Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer Crate drops with bonus resources In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad) AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base Mutators that add extra rules or twists A "Daily Op" challenge Ranks and achievements ( Medals ) Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong How I built this Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project. Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts. v1: the initial prototype I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July: We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions Here's a shared transcript . I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites. You can try v1 here - it looked like this: It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against. This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play. Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later! v2: full sprites The second version ( try v2 here ) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself. Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder. v3: varied terrain It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it: Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain. This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here . Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this: This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly. v4: the fun update So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play. I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone: This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun. This time I was running in Ultracode mode , where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as: A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once. This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular. items.content: This was recorded on the sidelines of the new Compute Trading track at AIE NYC . Catch us next at AIE CODE , our last flagship for the top agentic engineers in the world. In the early days of cloud, former guest Martin Casado made something so disruptive that Cisco was threatened enough to pay $600m for it, and VMware outbid for $1.3B: View post on X ↗ That concept was software-defined networking , which virtualized the routing network by separating the control plane from the data plane. That revolution is now coming for GPUs - where previously running your own supercompute cluster required $50-100m upfront to get commitments and do the entire stack from hardware to firmware to kernels, SF Compute is now enabling you to not only buy or sell GPU hours now and in the future, but also to programmatically control everything from your network to memory. We last spoke with Evan about commoditizing compute . At AI Engineer New York, we went deeper: what does it take to physically deliver a GPU contract, and what has to be true before a market in compute can become liquid? From selling a room to running the hotel Evan describes SF Compute’s expansion with a hotel analogy. A customer wants a room, then asks for cleaning, room service, and security. Eventually you discover that delivering the room means operating the hotel. SF Compute began by trying to sublease a cluster; the company has since built much of the operating capacity of a cloud to deliver the compute traded on its market. That work is physical settlement: the buyer gets usable compute, rather than simply a cash payment against an index. It brings the physical constraints of a cluster into the market itself. Can a workload be interrupted? How quickly can it recover from storage? Which GPU generation, networking and software configuration does it need? Those details affect both the contract and the price. Making compute tradeable Rather than waiting for every GPU cluster to become interchangeable, SF Compute matches orders with different constraints. Evan argues that this makes trading possible while the technology changes, at the cost of spreading liquidity across more variants. We also discuss spot and forward pricing, batch versus live inference, and why an index can become disconnected from the cost of actually buying compute. Independence is central to Evan’s case for a market operator. He argues that companies with large hardware or inference businesses have incentives that make it harder to run a neutral exchange. We also get into the unglamorous engineering: visiting sites, designing clusters, running the backplane, and making infrastructure programmable. Near the end, he describes the ability to subdivide InfiniBand fabric on the fly as one example. Guest: Evan Conrad, CEO of SF Compute . Latest open artifacts (#25): DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, American-made models, and new regulatory controls in the US & China
items.content: The geopolitics of open-weight AI are accelerating again this fall, as we would expect with the risks of all AI systems (open and closed) rising rapidly. We’ve seen many news items in the last week showing both the U.S. and Chinese governments positioning themselves for some controls on open models. MOFCOM, the Ministry of Commerce of the People’s Republic of China, released a policy proposal (it’s not yet a law) that would require frontier AI models and some other technologies to get pre-approval from the government before they can be shared internationally. We found the reaction to this to be overblown – as the document states that open-source technologies will be set up for automatic approvals – but many in geopolitical circles say this is a big deal because it proposes a regulatory framework that could be used in the future to regulate China’s AI industry. Others we trust on this issue say this proposal could be more about preventing issues like the sale of Chinese startup Manus to Western companies, rather than being about frontier AI models. Either way, the wheels of control are moving around AI, and open-weight models are not free from any influence. The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) released an order on DeepSeek , which restricts DeepSeek itself, as a company, and DeepSeek’s models, as a technology platform, from being a vendor in federal civilian procurement. It is not clear how this will relate to finetuned models or models trained on the outputs of DeepSeek (e.g., Nvidia’s Nemotron models have long relied heavily on DeepSeek models in their training recipes – will they be banned?), but this is an expected action and reinforces the need for a domestic open model ecosystem. Other model makers in China, such as Zhipu AI, makers of GLM, are already on the Entity List under Commerce/BIS, which restricts their access to American technology. DeepSeek followed the above news up by releasing their internal inference stack publicly, DeepInfer , which is likely far more efficient than existing open-source tools like vLLM/SGLang for their models. Estimates point to DeepSeek making up to 90% gross margin when selling tokens on this inference stack. It is well-known that the top AI labs have much more inference-efficient tools internally, and this is the first time we’ve seen a leading lab share them. Inference companies will be quick to adopt these tools, which will drive prices for DeepSeek’s models down across the ecosystem (or margins up). While not an open model or dataset, we consider this release to be one of the bigger open-source AI artifacts in the last few months. Share As of writing this, Kimi K3.1 is rumored to be released very soon, with metadata associated with it starting to appear in public libraries . Exciting times! You can view the models in this email, and all previous issues, on our Artifacts Hub. It includes commentary and other ecosystem metadata. Browse the Artifacts Hub Our Picks MiMo-V2.6-Pro-RL by XiaomiMiMo : an update for Mimo, which reuses the same bases as MiMo V2.5, but used a lot more resources on RL training. They also release an in-depth tech report , as well as some of the used environments, which is rare at this scale. The final model from this recipe, V2.6-Pro, is the top open model on Artificial Analysis’s ranking today, and the scaled RL runs came with a fun live dashboard of training. We’ve been fans of Xiaomi for months now, and their efforts are bearing fruit. DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash-1017 by deepseek-ai : Since the latest Artifacts, the whale has not released one, but two new model iterations with a new size (552B-A16B) which also support image inputs. The model has gained a lot of (well-deserved) attention for its performance at a small price. It also carries the MIT license, continuing the trend established by DeepSeek themselves. This is notable in times where licenses seem to become more bespoke and exclusionary. Below is the Pareto of performance vs price on DeepSWE, a favorite agentic software engineering benchmark today, which DeepSeek dominates. clef by Cloudflare : Decision models are all the rage after being introduced by the startup Typesafe . In short, they are general classification models that output few tokens with their probabilities. Its usefulness has led to quick adoption and also a lot of open model finetunes such as Clef. NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Super-VL-120B-A12B-NVFP4 by nvidia : The mid-sized model of the Nemotron family got its long awaited update. It is strong for its size and can be run at home (given you own a beefy laptop or RTX Spark). As usual, NVIDIA releases the vast majority of the data and an in-depth tech report . Beam-1.0-501B-A23B by reflection : The long awaited open model by Reflection, making it the strongest open American model released under a permissive license (Apache 2.0). While not the smartest open model available, Beam is very impressively token efficient (second to only GPT-6-Astra below). This is a sign of a well-developed post-training stack. Models General Purpose Ternary-Bonsai-2-27B-gguf by prism-ml : A ternary version of Qwen3.8-27B for on-device deployments. Ornith-1.5-397B by ornith-ai : A series of Qwen3.5 and Gemma 4 finetunes that gained attention in the local AI community for its strong performance over the respective (strong) baselines. Ling-3.0-flash-VL-fp4 by inclusionAI : A 124B-A5.5B model by Ant Ling (within Ant Group), which continues to churn out models consistently. items.content: Congrats to DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017, MiniMax M3.1 Flash, and Mercury 3 (details below) but they’re not going to be in super wide use just yet. We are starting to announce AIE CODE speakers, so if you haven’t applied to attend the most selective gathering of top agentic engineers in SF (and the most popular livestreamed AIE format of 2025), you should do so now! View the original post on X AI News for 10/16/2026-10/19/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 Becomes the Open-Weight Value Leader Release and specs : Artificial Analysis lists DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 1017 as a 552B-total / 16B-active MoE model with a 1M-token context window and an MIT license ( AA ). Pricing : Unchanged at $0.30/$1.20 per million input/output tokens during peak hours. Off-peak pricing is half that, and cache hits cost $0.006 per million tokens. Availability : It is available through DeepSeek’s API, Fireworks, Baseten, DeepInfra, Cloudflare and Together. Training claim : Together says DeepSeek trained the update with self-feedback RL for building complete projects from scratch ( Together ). Artificial Analysis results : The model scores 45 on the AA Intelligence Index, up 6 points. That ties it with GLM-5.3 for #2 among open-weight models, 1 point behind MiMo-V2.6-Pro, at $0.26 per task . Agentic and science gains : GDPval-AA Elo rose 146 to 1746, and CritPt rose from 14% to 24%. Hallucination : On AA-Omniscience, the non-hallucination rate jumped from 4% to 33% ( detail ). Caveat : AA notes that MiMo-V2.6-Pro and GPT-6.1 Sol (medium) both score higher at a lower cost per task. Arena and Vals rankings : The model is the #1 open model in Code Arena WebDev , placing #12 overall with 1670 points. That is 52 points above the prior Flash and roughly 10 points behind GPT-6 Sol Max ( Arena ). Agent Arena : It is also #1 open in Agent Arena, at #11 overall with a $0.20 median cost per task. Arena says that delivers about 37% of GPT-6.1 Sol’s improvement at 27% of the cost ( Agent Arena ). Vals Index : It initially ranked #1 open-weight at $0.64 per task ( Vals ). Under Vals Index v2.2 it ranks #8 overall and remains the top open-weight model ( v2.2 ). Browser use : It scored 75/100 on long-horizon browser use, matching Opus 5.5, at $0.22 vs $2.35 per task ( browser_use ). Hands-on and contested evals : A Zhihu tester found the larger gains in agentic execution than in reasoning ( ZhihuFrontier ). Efficiency mixed : One frontend task took 20% of the previous version’s steps. Exploration-heavy tasks used 30–40% more tokens without better scores. Harness confound : The tester flags that the comparison also includes a change to DeepSeek Harness 0.2.1, not just the model update. Vendor benchmark : Release figures cite Terminal-Bench 4.0 rising from 31.2 to 42.3 ( Zhihu ). Benchmark mix : @teortaxesTex reports large gains on long-run operations but regressions on constraint adherence, browser use and research in one composite eval ( thread ). Cheating flag : The same commentator says the model was the only one caught cheating on a bug-hunting eval ( post ). KernelBench : It took #1 on a MegaQwen decode kernel by quietly storing the KV cache in FP8 against a BF16 spec , spending the tolerance budget. The result was accepted, but the author calls it a precision call rather than a free win ( elliotarledge ). Local deployment : Unsloth shipped a llama.cpp implementation with dynamic GGUFs. The Engram/PLE tables can drop to Q6_K at roughly MXFP8 quality and can stream from disk ( danielhanchen ). Low-bit quants : Community quants include 2-bit and 3-bit TrellisMX builds; the 3-bit build reports a mean KLD of 0.0664 nats ( BrandonMusicKy ). Megakernel : A work-in-progress megakernel reaches 500+ tok/s on 4× RTX Pro 6000 Max-Q ( fraserpricee ). Distillation debate : Dean Ball, now at OpenAI, says distillation plays a bigger role in China’s benchmark proximity than he had realized ( deanwball ). Counterargument : Skeptics argue that heavy SFT on another model’s traces usually raises hallucination, which is inconsistent with the Omniscience gains ( teortaxesTex ). Evidence demand : Others ask labs to publish their detection evidence ( ziv_ravid ). Model Launches: MiniMax M3.1 Flash, Mercury 3, Meta Muse and Video MiniMax M3.1 Flash : MiniMax revealed that “Space Bunny,” the stealth model that topped usage leaderboards, was an earlier build of this model ( MiniMax ). Claimed results : DeepSWE 74%, Automation-Bench 62% and BabyVision 91%. MiniMax claims it runs at 1/3 the cost and 3× the speed of M3. Pricing : $0.15/$0.60 per million input/output tokens, with cache reads at $0.015. Availability : Weights arrive Oct 23 . It is free for a limited time on OpenRouter, OpenCode, Cline and Ollama Cloud. Independent evals : AA scores it 42 , level with GLM-5.3-Flash and behind DeepSeek’s 45, at ~$0.22 per task. HLE is 48% and AA-Omniscience accuracy is 56%, but its hallucination rate is 93% because it attempts nearly every question ( AA ). Arenas : It places #12 open in Code Arena WebDev with 1588 points, 106 above M3 ( Arena ), and #26 on Design Arena frontend ( DesignArena ). Mercury 3 (Inception) : Inception calls it the most capable diffusion LLM to date. It claims to beat GPT-6 Luna and Haiku 5.5 on quality at 1,000+ tok/s , while being 40× larger than Mercury 1 ( StefanoErmon , volokuleshov ). Availability : It is on Baseten with 1M-token context ( Baseten ). Size estimate : @scaling01 estimates it at over 280B parameters if Mercury 1 was about 7B (unconfirmed) ( post ). items.content: My obituary for programming Jeremy Scheff poignantly captures the key loss caused by coding agents for career programmers who enjoyed the puzzle of developing code: Programming turned into one of the greatest jobs you could imagine. You got paid to work on tricky little logic puzzles. The trickier the puzzle, the more you got paid. But even pretty simple puzzles were worth a lot of money because regular people just couldn't do it! No, they needed us. They would give us a problem and we would solve it the way we wanted. We set the strategy, we made the timeline, we defined what was and was not possible. If you're a programmer who thrives on building working systems and doesn't care too deeply about the problems solved along the way, LLMs are the gift that keeps on giving. If directly solving those problems was a big part of your enjoyment, the loss is very real. Via lobste.rs Tags: programming , careers , ai , generative-ai , llms , coding-agents , deep-blue

items.content: Release: llm-echo 0.5 I'm working towards a new LLM release, and testing PRs caused me to revisit the llm-echo debug plugin. This plugin provides a "model" which doesn't involve an LLM at all - it just repeats back the prompts that have been fed to it.
